item.title: How to Play Levia in Silver Age
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|competitive

How to Play Levia in Silver Age

Satiate your hunger with Karol's guide to the returning Shadow Brute!

By Karol Ruszkiewicz

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Levia has shown up as a huge contender this Silver Age season, securing three placements in the Top 8 thanks to the efforts of Jacob Clements, Francesco Giorgio, and Kilian Schellekens. I've scoured through these decklists to find which cards are must-includes and what tech the different players have sprinkled in.

Levia already had some great common and rare cards in the past. Dread Screamer, Boneyard Marauder, Endless Maw, and Graveling Growl have all been incredible at punching through raw damage. However, the way these work, it takes some time to get enough cards into the graveyard, let alone enough 6-power attack action cards to consistently play these out while satisfying Levia's blood debt.

In terms of previous equipment, Hooves of the Shadowbeast has been a monster of a leg piece, being extremely flexible in granting not only an attack go again, but also an action point as long as you have a card to banish. That's it. Banish a 6-power card and you can convert your boots into a clean action point. Beaten Trackers...but better?

More recently, Compendium of Rathe introduced further power cards in the form of Embraforged Gauntlet, Engulfing Shadows, and Pound of Flesh.

On the Brute side, we also received some top-tier pieces of equipment that play really well into Levia's game plan. Buzzard Helm helps fix awkward hands, such as drawing four reds, while also filling up the graveyard to enable the old-school Shadow Brute attacks.

Predatory Plating also offers great defensive value and a precious resource when it matters. And it can matter a lot.

Levia's curve often uses 2-cost cards with go again, meaning two blues are perfect for playing out three of these in a row, often performing her iconic attack for 6, then 6, then 6. However, sometimes you're only able to attack twice, and 4 can be an awkward amount of pitch. This is why we see these lists include Vigorous Smashup in yellow and blue, with some running all six available copies. Vigor and top-deck manipulation are crucial for smoothing out certain turns, especially when combined with the toys Levia just received in Usurp the Shadow Throne...

So what makes Levia so good all of a sudden?

Firstly, it's the new attacks.

Big Bonkers

What's better than some over-rate attacks? A whole lot more over-rate attacks! Not only that, but ones that don't require a busy graveyard to get going.

Feeding Frenzy and Feasting Shadowbeast are all-star attacks that not only match the efficiency of the Monarch attacks, but are also much easier to enable. Their effects are satisfied by any banish, not just their own. This means they make great follow-up cards and can also be enabled by cards like Hex Gauntlet and Cleave the Heavens.

Gates to i'Arathael

Cleave the Heavens isn't just a pretty face. It creates one of the most important components of Levia's toolkit: Gates to i'Arathael, a token that unlocks "free" cards from banish. As the game goes on, you'll have more and more juicy targets for these Gates, allowing you to throw out attacks with unparalleled efficiency.

Being able to convert a single blue into a Feasting Shadowbeast for 8 while satisfying blood debt is incredible, especially in Silver Age. Gates are particularly effective against slower decks that give you time to set up big turns and the space to build a hefty banish zone. I recommend leaning further into setting up Gates with cards like Rites of Nightfall, Countdown to Extinction, and more copies of Cleave the Heavens if your local metagame likes to take it slow.

Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger

The big demon makes his way into Silver Age! Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger offers an amazing package against a wide range of decks. Cards like Goremass Summoning, Beckoning Hunger, and Rumbling Hunger are the main ways to get the demon into the arena, and that is one scary on-hit. If your opponent lets this one through, it can take over the game.

While Gates offer a similar effect, not having to pitch that extra resource and having the effect on tap means you can continue playing free cards from banish, as long as you feed the beast, that is.

Blasmophet's upkeep requires you to continue banishing Shadow cards. Luckily, on your turn you're most likely doing that anyway to satisfy your hero ability. However, it's a bit trickier to do so on your opponent's turn. Some cards fulfill this condition themselves. Cleave the Heavens, Embraforged Gauntlet, and Engulfing Shadows all banish Shadow cards in one form or another.

Some cards also benefit from having a Blasmophet in play. The most played one is Consuming Command, a power play if you have it in your banish zone while controlling a Blasmophet. For 1 resource, you get to attack for 6 with go again, and the best thing is that if you continue to load it with graveyard-banishing effects, you can continue to attack with it. Most lists run only one copy, as that seems to be all you need to get the loop going.

Metagaming

There are a few cards that stood out to me, as they made some lists but not others.

Kilian's build seems the most resilient to fatigue strategies. Including two copies of Howl from Beyond opens up a constant loop of power. You play out the Howl, buff up your attack, then banish it from the graveyard with a Dread Screamer or Boneyard Marauder.

Jacob Clements is a big fan of Agility. Including a Test of Agility and Clash of Agility means that, as long as he can win those clashes, he can make these already incredibly efficient attacks even better by giving them go again. Smashback Alehorn offers even more go again and extra power, making it a great setup card for creating explosive turns.

Another point of contention is whether the lists should run Consuming Lash or Consuming Strength. As a general rule of thumb, I'd say go again is more likely to be useful against slower decks, while the extra +2 power pairs nicely with on-hit attacks like Rumbling Hunger and Beckoning Hunger, especially against aggressive decks that don't want to be defending.

Closing Thoughts

Despite just entering this new metagame, these players have turned up with incredibly tuned decks and a strategy for anything their opponents might throw at them.

I hope you got plenty of useful information on how to pilot Levia, because she is not only a highly competitive deck, but also a delightful puzzle to solve each and every game.

item.title: Buyer's Guide to Disney Lorcana's Hyperia City
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|finance

Buyer's Guide to Disney Lorcana's Hyperia City

Which products should you be buying from Disney Lorcana's latest set?

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 7, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

I've always had a soft spot for Coco. 

A film from 2017 may be a little too late in the Disney pipeline to stoke my nostalgia, but I first watched this one while leaning over in my airplane seat to see what was on the next monitor over. Could I have simply loaded up the film on the monitor in front of me? Sure, but I was too enamoured with the music and fireworks to consider things such as practicality or posture. I also thought my neighbour might look at me weird, but so it goes. 

Dia de los Muertos lends itself to such wonderful iconography, and it isn't lost on me that Hyperia City is entering the game shortly before the Spanish holiday. Disney Lorcana's latest set is headlined by iconic characters and songs from Coco, mixed in with a wicked blend of fan-favorite glimmers and returning franchises. If the rest of 2026 is anything to go by, it's bound to be a smash hit. 

Admittedly, that's part of what worries me. Disney Lorcana has been exploding in popularity since the joint release of Wilds Unknown and Toy Story 5 earlier this year, leading to a huge influx in collectors and unprecedented demand for product. That means it's easier than ever to get swept up in FOMO or simply assign your budget to snapping up the first product you see. 

I'm hopeful we can do better than that — or I'm going to try and help us do better than that, at least. 

There are a few different products on the market for Hyperia City, and I want to make sure you're picking up the correct one for your needs and price point. I also want to make sure you've got your finger on the pulse when it comes to expected price point: hype is always going to be driving that number up as we head closer to release, but only you get to decide what you're happy to purchase at. I find being informed to be the best first step for that. 

It's also worth remembering that this is the final set before the introduction of Collector Boosters to Disney Lorcana, and as such the last time that the product spread will look like this. Will that lead to less purchases and lower prices while people hold their budget for the upcoming collector boom? Unlikely. It is worth keeping in mind, however. 

With all that said, let us dive into a town where metro meets fantastical. Here's a punchy pocket guide to all products from Hyperia City. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Booster Pack

  • MSRP: $5.99 each
  • Current Market Value (as of 10/05/2026): $14.95

Hype(ria) is the name of the game when it comes to single booster packs, which have been comfortably selling for between $15 - $20 during the countdown to pre-release. Big box sleeved boosters don't exist on the market yet, which definitely plays a role in that.

Single booster packs are always the cheapest way to get a small taste of a new set without heavy investment, but this is a little bit ludicrous in my opinion. Recent sets like Wilds Unknown and Attack of the Vine! have been holding steady at roughly $10 per booster since release. That's still almost 2x MSRP... but that's a whole lot better than 3x. 

I would chill on these until they're more in line with previous sets. That said, I will be using this price point as a measuring stick for the value proposition of other products in the set as we go. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Booster Box 

  • MSRP: $143.76
  • $143.76/24 Packs = $5.99 per pack
  • Current Market Value (as of 10/05/2026): $209
  • $209/24 Packs = $8.70 per pack

If you look at the price chart for Hyperia City booster boxes, you'll see that we hit the pre-release plateau towards the end of September and demand is about to start driving prices upwards again as we get closer to release. 

It's not difficult to see why either. Compared to buying individual booster packs, you're currently saving over six dollars per booster by buying an entire box. That's over one hundred and forty bucks: the MSRP of an entire box. 

Booster boxes typically work out to be the best value-for-money product when the dust settles if you're willing to make a higher level of investment, but this is night and day right now. If you can find a box at under $200, I'd be snapping it up. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Illumineer's Trove

  • MSRP: $49.99
  • $49.99/8 Packs = $6.25 per pack
  • Current Market Value (as of 10/05/2026): $111.93
  • $111.93/8 Packs = $13.99 per pack

For better or worse, the hype phase always inflates the prices on Illumineer's Troves. They're the favorite product of the community, and so they tend to draw more attention (and purchases) than anything else. 

Players love to collect these for their helpful mixture of storage box, booster packs and gameplay accessories. They're the middle-ground product for anybody looking for something bigger than a booster pack but smaller than an entire box. At MSRP, the additional goodies cost you about two dollars. I personally value them a little higher, but not fifty bucks higher. 

If you absolutely must have a trove, I don't expect these to fall off by much on the secondary market. If the extra goodies don't mean that much, you'll get much better booster value by purchasing something else. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City 2-Player Starter Set

  • MSRP: $29.99
  • Current Market Value (as of 10/05/2026): $68.57

This is only the second instalment of the 2-Player Starter Set, which debuted earlier this year in Wilds Unknown. This is a gateway product designed to teach new players and casual enjoyers, offering a great onboarding product for anybody interested in Disney Lorcana. It includes everything you need for two players to get started with the game. 

The variant from Wilds Unknown is one of the few products that settled below MSRP in the end. While there are some unique foils inside the product that command some attention, I expect this set to be readily available shortly after release. Please don't spend almost $70 to obtain a copy. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Gift Box - Beast

  • MSRP: $29.99 each
  • $29.99/5 Packs = $5.99 per pack
  • Current Market Value (as of 10/05/2026): $69.59 each
  • $69.69/5 Packs = $13.91 per pack

It's worth noting that the Hyperia City Gift Box - Beast does not release at the same time as all of the other Hyperia City products. This won't arrive until the 13th of November — it's clearly more targeted towards that holiday shopping period. 

That means there's a little more time for preorders to settle here, but I am expecting this gift set to be hotly contested. These "glimmer foil" promo cards have seen a huge popularity spike as of late and I don't expect Beast - Snowfield Troublemaker to be any different. 

If Elsa - The Fifth Spirit is anything to go by, you can expect the promo to be worth a solid $10. In that world, any copy of this product you can find at MSRP is an absolute steal. I'd be very happy picking up copies at $40-$50 each. They even remain better value than a trove right now if you don't mind the wait. 

I expect to see these flying out as parents begin hunting down stocking fillers, so don't wait around if you're desperate to have one. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Playmats

  • MSRP (Stitch - Snowboarder and Miguel Rivera): $19.99
  • Current Market Price (as of 10/05/2026): ~$40 each (Stitch - Snowboarder and Miguel Rivera)
  • Current Market Price (as of 10/05/2026): ??? (I2I Foil Park Exclusive)

As you've come to expect from each new Disney Lorcana release, there's a smattering of new accessories hitting the market too. Stitch - Snowboarder and Miguel Rivera get the playmat treatment this time around, and I'm expecting to see both readily available at roughly MSRP shortly after release. 

The I2I playmat is a bit of a different beast, however. This mat is a park exclusive. That means it'll only be available at specific Disney locations in limited quantities. These limited-time-only collectible mats consistently command between $150 - $200 if you're looking to secure one on the secondary market, so I'd be sure to snag one if you find yourself on a Disney holiday sometime soon. 

Disney Lorcana Hyperia City Pre-Release Kits

I also wanted to tack on a quick note about a product you won't be able to find on the TCGplayer marketplace just yet. You can expect us to offer Hyperia City pre-release kits about one week after the in-store events have ended. 

These products are designed to cultivate in-store play, which remains the best way to pick up new cards and play casual games with your local community. We're not in the business of undermining that — you should go and support your LGS if you can. 

That said, not everybody is lucky enough to have a local game store in travelling distance, so we'll make sure these are up and on the site shortly afterwards. Each kit contains six booster packs, some accessories and an exclusive hot-stamped pre-release promo card to mark the occasion. Personally, I'm hoping for Above the Crowd. 

If you want to find an event near you, check out the Ravensburger Store Locator to find your nearest locations. If you'd like to make my week, tag me on socials when you're sharing your photos of the event!

item.title: The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/07/2026
item.description:
Pokémon|finance

The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/07/2026

30th Celebration singles plummet, but the anniversary has produced some unexpected winners.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 7, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

"What's Your Favorite?"

No, that's not a rhetorical question. In fact, it's not a question at all—it's the cycle of promotional cards that were first given away to retail stores and passed out to customers to celebrate the release of Pitch Black a couple of months ago. Most recently, the What's Your Favorite? Mewtwo was released (I personally picked one up while scoring a drop at Target), and with more eyes than ever on Pokémon thanks to the 30th Celebration release, that was all it took to drive attention to—and drive up prices on—this set of cards.

Along with Mewtwo, which is selling today for about $17, this promo cycle also included a trio of cards that all leapt up in price over the weekend:

Giant jump for Primarina, which went from $10 up to a new high of $23. Zarude had a somewhat more muted climb, going from $28 up to $35. Meanwhile, Armarouge started off the most expensive of them all at $30, and after a wild weekend it's up to a $42 Market Price.

There seem to be more chances at Mewtwo on the way, with Best Buy, Gamestop, Barnes & Noble, and even Macy's all getting in on the action (as well as EB Games in Canada). I will say that I was excited to take my five-year-old to the "event" at Target that was supposed to include activities for little kids, and instead it was just a line for the drop. A bit disappointing. But overall, as someone who has been on the front lines for this release, the excitement is not dying down, even if the prices are.

And they are. The average 30th Celebration hit has been dropping like a rock in price over the last week, with the beautiful Mew ex 152 taking a plunge from $150 down to just below $100. Night Pikachu 150 dipped from $90 to $65 and actually fell below the $70 Gengar ex 154, which fell precipitously itself, from over $100.

Speaking of Mewtwo, who would have guessed that the Futuristic Rare printing of the Psychic boss would dip as low as $40? Yet it has, and I think we'll see even more weakness from it as more and more 30th Celebration hits the market. It certainly seems like no amount of product released could sate demand from long lines and campouts happening across the United States, but all that pack cracking will be felt in the prices of the singles. Futuristic Mew has fared only a little better, settling in around $60 after starting the week off at $90.

As for the extreme top end of the set, the RBG Mews? At the top end listings for the Red variant are all in the $5,000 range, with completed sales both below and above that number in the last fortnight. Meanwhile, both the blue and green variants are selling in the $3,500 range. Even among the top end of the top end Mews, it appears there is a pecking order.

This is one of those Pokémon stories that's hard to believe. Gengar Lv.X from the 2009 Arceus release has unsurprisingly always been worth a decent amount of money. Being a mega-popular Pokémon from a relatively dead era of Pokémon sets was good enough to put Lv. X Gengar at $60-80 for most of the past five years.

But Gengar began climbing in Summer 2025, and pretty much hasn't stopped since. It hit $150 this time a year ago, jumped again to $300 at the beginning of the year, and made it all the way to $500 by August. Fast forward another six weeks and the last Near Mint copy of Lv. X Gengar sold for well over $1,000. The new Market Price officially says $680, but make no mistake, these are running right around $1,000 a listing right now on TCGplayer.

Slowking Prime from Undaunted jumped from $70 up to $90 this week, which is the top of a climb that's been building in momentum all year. Slowking has climbed from $30 back at the beginning of the Summer to over $150 for a Near Mint copy today.

Likewise, Garchomp from the 2009 release Supreme Victors has been on a tear recently. It's up from $50 a few months ago, with the most recent Near Mint listing bringing the card's price closer to $100.

The second Jirachi to climb in price in as many weeks, this time it's the Celestial Storm printing of Jirachi Prism Star that is taking a jump in price. The Steel-type Pokémon began the year just under $10, but began to climb several months into 2026 and had reached as high as $15 by the end of the summer. But Jirachi has been on a continued run ever since, and today you're looking at Near Mint copies beginning around $75.

At the top end of Celestial Storm are several cards making their way up slowly, in fact. Rayquaza-GX leads the way in that regard, going from $300 up to over $350 in the last six weeks, while Articuno-GX is up to over $70 and Scizor-GX is now pushing $100 for the first time. These are pretty incremental moves, but given the leap on Jirachi Prism Star, it wouldn't be a shock for any of these to take a more drastic leap in price in the coming weeks.

It's a busy time in the Pokémon world as 30th Celebration works its way into the ever-changing market, and it's a lot of fun to follow—see you next week!

item.title: The Top 10 Most Expensive Manga-Style Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Japan's Original Artwork Collection
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|finance

The Top 10 Most Expensive Manga-Style Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Japan's Original Artwork Collection

Some classic style comes to Yu-Gi-Oh for the 30th anniversary.

By Ken Nishi

|

Published Oct 7, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

The Original Artwork Collection is the latest Yu-Gi-Oh set to come out in Japan, and it has quickly become one of the hottest sets in the OCG. It celebrates the 30th anniversary of the manga and introduces the next batch of Grand Master Rares, causing duelists to scramble to get their hands on packs to crack open.

One aspect of the set that some duelists may have overlooked is the new manga-style cards! These cards look quite different from the usual layout, with a white frame, black stars and no attribute or type on the card. They're meant to look like the card layouts used back in the original manga! Despite the differences, these cards are legal for play in the OCG and have the same stats and effects as their regular counterparts. Each card has four different versions: a monochrome black-and-white version and a colored version, with each available as both an Ultra Rare and Secret Rare.

The Most Expensive Manga-Style Yu-Gi-Oh Cards

The unique appearance of these manga-style cards has swiftly caught the attention of collectors around the world! Unfortunately, we don't know when the cards will be brought over to the TCG, so for now, the Original Artwork Collection is the only place you'll be able to pull these cards from packs. For this article, we're taking a look at the Top 10 most expensive manga-style cards at the moment. Since Japanese cards aren't listed on TCGplayer, we'll be looking at recently completed eBay sales to determine what these cards are currently selling for.

#10 Skull Servant

Kicking off our list is Skull Servant! This unassuming Zombie made its debut in the first core set, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon, and has since received many waves of support that can punish unsuspecting duelists. Skull Servant duelists are typically hardcore fans of the theme, so picking up a few of these would be a nice addition to the undead army. These aren't too pricey, either, with the Secret Rare coloured versions coming in at about $10 a pop!  

#9 Harpie's Feather Duster

While the Original Artwork Collection features some of the oldest cards in the game, that doesn't mean that some of them aren't playable! Harpie's Feather Duster is a card that is Limited to one in both the TCG and OCG, which means that the card is still usable by duelists in Asia. The card already has two different artworks available in the TCG, but this printing could fill out that missing page in your binder quite nicely. For such an iconic card, picking up a copy for around $10 is quite a steal!

#8 Mirror Force

Speaking of iconic cards, the number eight spot on our list goes to Mirror Force! This was always one of Yugi's most devastating cards, and it felt like Yugi was guaranteed to win the duel whenever he flipped it face-up. That said, the original artwork of Mirror Force doesn't differ too much from the version that we got in Metal Raiders; in fact, this printing might even be a little bit flatter. It's still an amazing card that's awesome to see in its original form, but a $13 price tag is almost surprising given how loved the card is!

#7 Buster Blader

One of Yugi's most iconic monsters from Battle City, Buster Blader was an important monster that helped Yugi to beat both Strings and Kaiba! This artwork of the card is less intimidating than the original, but it doesn't take away from his intimidating red eyes glaring at you through the card. If you happen to pull a Dark Paladin - Wave-Motion from the Original Artwork Collection, this artwork could be a nice companion piece at only $14.

#6 Harpie Lady

It wouldn't be a top 10 most expensive card list without at least one card charging the waifu tax, and in this case, it's Harpie Lady! Mai Valentine's signature monster takes the sixth spot, and this particular artwork is much closer up than any other Harpie Lady variant. With Harpie Lady - Elegant Egotist making its debut in the same set, you can easily swarm your binder with Harpie monsters, and this one comes in at $14.

#5 Gaia the Fierce Knight

Just making its way into the top five, it's Gaia the Fierce Knight! One of Yugi's key monsters throughout the Duelist Kingdom series, it seems that fans of the original anime have been keen to pick up this particular artwork of the card. While Gaia does have very similar artwork in the Millennium Pack, that particular version was never printed in the TCG as a holo, so this printing is a nice upgrade for collectors. The colored Secret Rare version is currently sitting at just over the $14 mark!

#4 Jinzo

Although the artwork doesn't differ too much from the one we received in Pharaoh's Servant, there's something eerily intimidating about the manga-style version of Jinzo, with its polished metal and darker background. Then again, the Japanese name for this card is "Android - Psycho Shocker", which sounds much more menacing than Jinzo. It's not the most meta-relevant card anymore, but for a while, this card was a staple in Goat Format decks. If you're playing casually with friends and want your list to stand out that little bit more, you can pick up this copy for about $19.

#3 Dark Magician

The ultimate wizard in terms of attack and defense, Dark Magician surprisingly comes in at the number three spot! While most of the new artworks are available for the first time in the Original Artwork Collection, Dark Magician was actually available previously. In Japan, it was part of a campaign held back in 2021, while in the TCG, the card was a difficult-to-pull chase card in Battle of Chaos. For that reason, this particular printing feels less exclusive. However, it's still Dark Magician, and it still carries a price tag of around $60!

#2 Red-Eyes Black Dragon

Surprisingly coming in at the number two spot and making its way past Dark Magician, we have Red-Eyes Black Dragon! Joey's signature monster just received a retrain in Beyond the Brave, and that seems to have rejuvenated interest from fans of Joey, pushing the price of the manga-style colored Secret Rares to around $75. Red-Eyes is still one of the most intimidating monsters in the game, with its dark colors really giving it an intimidating feeling. In this set, it's only topped by one monster, and of course, that is…

#1 Blue-Eyes White Dragon

Could it really be anything else? The legendary dragon tops the list of the most expensive manga-style cards from the Original Artwork Collection, significantly higher than Red-Eyes or Dark Magician at about $170 per copy. It's not the most expensive Blue-Eyes around, but it's certainly one of the most unique, and if you're a Blue-Eyes fan, it's definitely something you have to add to your collection.

With so many iconic cards receiving this unique treatment, it'll be interesting to see how these manga-style cards hold up as more copies enter the market. It will also be interesting to see if we receive these cards in the TCG, and how they will affect the prices of their OCG counterparts.

item.title: The Most Exciting New Cards From Riftbound's Radiance
item.description:
Riftbound|competitive

The Most Exciting New Cards From Riftbound's Radiance

Pop stars, time travel and... hidden demons? I think I saw a TV show about this...

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 8, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

"Exciting" is such a double-edged word. After all, what excites me may terrify or bore you. Each individual player and collector will have different things that get our blood pumping, but that's a big part of what makes reveal season so cool to me. 

TCGs offer such a wide variety of options to tickle your fancy both across games and within them. I have fallen in love with the resource-bending tempo gameplay of Annie, Dark Child and the sheer velocity of a deck like Kennen, Heart of the Tempest, while simultaneously groaning at turn three copies of Dazzling Aurora or Zhonya's Hourglass curving into Stellacorn Herder. 

I can't deny the joy on the face of the people committing these war crimes against me, though. How cool is that? 

I think just over two weeks before the release of Radiance is the correct time to talk about exciting. Card reveals are dropping every day, and the gears of my mind are beginning to turn. Perhaps you find yourself excited that your favorite League of Legends character is entering the game? Maybe Neeko, Bleeding In has you reeling, or the new ultimate Packed Amphitheater would be the grail of your collection? 

There are a million reasons to get excited about Radiance — and I want to take some time to talk about mine. These are the newest card reveals that have me most excited so far. 

Chronobreak

To fully understand why I'm so excited about Chronobreak, you need to both know a little bit about me and take a closer look at Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time. 

When I was still cutting my teeth over in Magic: the Gathering, I made a bit of a name for myself playing decks that revolved around the card Ephemerate. The value gained by "flickering" cards out of play to retrigger them or save them from destruction is one of my favorite things to do in any card game. Strangely enough, that seems to be Ekko's playstyle. 

Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time allows you to cheat units into play at a much cheaper cost if you're willing to both empower him and allow the unit to die at the end of the turn. This works just fine with Deathknell effects like Ruined Rex or Ferrous Forerunner, but Chronobreak joins Temporal Breach as a cheap way to reset that death trigger.

If you banish and replay a unit, the game treats it like a new object, so it won't need to be killed at the end of turn. Of course, this is equally powerful with on-play abilities to double-dip on their powers at the same energy cost as they would have been without Ekko. It's also worth noting that Chronobreak allows you to pull back to base, making it particularly nasty with accelerate units like Thousand-Tailed Watcher. 

I'm sure this deck already wanted to dabble in the Brynhir Thundersong + Temporal Breach combo, so additional ways to flicker and abuse those flickers seems like a slam dunk to me. 

Trifarian Captain

Good enough. Welcome back, Stacked Deck! 

As much as I'm joking a little, Trifarian Captain theoretically jumps straight back into Kennen, Heart of the Tempest to re-enable Nocturne, Horrifying power spikes. It also cleanly searches up anything from Seal of Discord to Fizz, Trickster. While it doesn't fuel Rhasa the Sunderer anywhere near as cleanly as the now-banned cantrip, I do think this card can do some work.

That's to say nothing of its place in non-Kennan decks. A two drop that replaces itself is always going to be solid, but this is one that'll improve with time. Each new fear or cheap unit makes Trifarian Captain more appealing to play, and that's the type of card I always want to be watching. 

Bedeviling Stranger

Alright, maybe "excited" isn't the right word for this one. I'll be playing it in my purple decks, make no mistake... but it is a little terrifying. 

Bedeviling Stranger reads like a potent card for Evelynn, Agony's Embrace to utilize, but I'm more interested in the tension it creates alongside Switcheroo. Much like Rebuke or Fight or Flight before it, it's incredibly difficult to play around one without getting blown out by the other. 

If you send in one unit to contest the opposing battlefield, you get blown out by Switcheroo being hidden. If you send in more than one, you get annihilated by a hidden Bedeviling Stranger. I'm personally not a huge fan of these damned-if-you-do-damned-if-you-don't scenarios, but I do think it's going to be very powerful in a variety of purple decks. Vex, Gloomist feels like a huge winner when it comes to this card. 

At the very least, it's going to be really frustrating to play into at times. 

Last Caress

Alright Riot, be honest. Who forgot to put a power cost on this thing?! 

This is a cripplingly powerful specialization. The mere existence of Last Caress means that each hidden card you control could theoretically contest any battlefield at any time, causing untold combat headaches for your opponent. It also allows you to pseudo-accelerate your units and contest battlefields when your opponent thinks they're safe. It's absurd. 

Last Caress also comes with the Ride the Wind caveat: it allows you to score in the opposing turn. By deploying a hidden unit to a different, uncontested battlefield (or heaven forbid, a battlefield that you can overwhelm!) and scoring a point before holding, you can really flip the point math of a game. 

This card is powerful, flashy and cheap. I don't see a world where you're not slamming three in every Evelynn, Agony's Embrace deck that you build.

Riven, Broken Blade

I want to note that (at time of writing), we haven't officially seen Riven's legend. That said, I think Riven, Broken Blade is probably a house regardless of what it does. 

Draven, Vanquisher showed us the power of having a four-cost, zero power machine in your champion zone. If there's a consistent way to have Riven entering ready (as her text would imply), she threatens to dominate battlefields between stuns and buffs. In fact, watching a movement-focused legend like Yasuo, Unforgiven ping Riven, Broken Blade around the arena has terrifying implications! 

My big concern for Riven outside of her corresponding legend is how difficult it is to fight Stellacorn Herder for the four-energy slot in deckbuilding. As a unit coming out of the champion zone, though? Seems really good. 

Consult the Heavens

Bruh. 

A one-cost Shield 2 feels like it could be backbreaking in Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman, Vex, Gloomist and K'Sante, Pride of Nazumah. It might honestly be good enough across the board because that's some absurd efficiency. 

That's before considering the half-a-card of value you gain from predicting. This extra line of text is particularly strong in Vex, Gloomist, who will get to control the card she draws from successfully holding. I'm happily slotting some number of these into my hold-focused green decks and never looking back. 

Coalesced Energy

Yoooooooo. We're getting support for my boy Renekton in the year 2026?! 

Coalesced Energy looks a little innocuous, but I think this card is capable of doing some obnoxious things. As a floor, it'll refund the power you spend to play it on turn two going first. That's a fine fail rate, but I'm more interested in the big, flashy stuff. 

Renekton, Butcher of the Sands is the obvious place for this, allowing you to play Coalesced Energy on turn one and actively accelerate your energy. I'm also interested in things like Hextech Anomaly or Chronobreak that allow you to spend power en-masse. 

Coalesced Energy feels unfair. It's just gonna take some tinkering to figure out exactly where. 

Runeblade Anvil

Runeblade Anvil also feels unfair. I'm not so sure about the tinkering part this time, though. 

Detonate was already sitting on thin ice after the whole Draven debacle, but the team chose to (correctly) take away Scrapheap instead. Runeblade Anvil steps into the hole left behind as the perfect gear to explode on command and achieve maximum velocity. It's probably even better with Pack of Wonders as a near-endless resource engine. Ridiculous. 

I expect to see the re-emergence of some number of purple/red "miracle" strategies once Runeblade Anvil enters the format. It just fits so cleanly into that style of gameplay. 

Avalanche

Falling Star isn't the only way to send your opponent's head spinning, it seems. The base is no longer as safe as it once was at the hands of Avalanche. 

I've got half an eye on any mass damage effects with Seraphine, Starry-Eyed Songstress entering the game. Having a consistent tool to bury any wayward tokens under a pile of ice is something I'm excited to have in the back pocket, but not something I'm expecting to redefine the format. 

Avalanche feels like a sweet sideboard card that'll fundamentally change how far some decks are willing to extend/retreat. Simply put, I love seeing cards like that. 

Resplendent Rostrum

Nasus, Curator of the Sands is feasting here. What an absurd pickup. 

Resplendent Rostrum almost reads like a custom card for this deck, triggering your legend ability, refunding its power cost, fuelling your hand with more gigantic things to slam and offering bonus might for your leftover Scuttle Crab or Lecturing Yordle. 

I also think Resplendent Rostrum has a place in bigger versions of Orianna, Lady of Clockwork, who will happily turn the gigantic monument into an eight might unit that can grant itself bonus might once it gets into a showdown. Frankly, I'm always down for sweet ramp payoffs that provide angles of attack other than Dazzling Aurora, so this card has me feeling all bubbly. 

Closing Thoughts

Radiance still has so many cards left to reveal at time of writing and I'm already buzzing like an old fridge. I find so much of the design in this set exciting, which felt like as good a reason to write an article as any. 

How are you feeling about Radiance? Are some other cards catching your attention? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: Wretched Ranks MTG Foundations Commander Upgrade Guide
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|Commander|budget|casual

Wretched Ranks MTG Foundations Commander Upgrade Guide

What is dead never dies.

By Tyler Berger

|

Published Oct 8, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Commander Upgrade

The five Magic Foundations Commander preconstructed decks are the latest beginner friendly way to jump into Magic: The Gathering's most popular format. Today, we're embracing our dark side with the Wretched Ranks deck! We're going to send an ever growing army of zombies at our opponents, or sacrifice our zombies for powerful abilities. It's okay, they never stay dead for long…

Wretched Ranks brings a ton of different ways to put many creatures on the field, going wide rather than going tall. That is, we want a high quantity of expendable creatures rather than a few really big ones. The first place you'll see that is with the deck's commander: Ghoulcaller Gisa.

Take Command of the Wretched Ranks

In Magic's story, Gisa is a ghoulcaller from the plane of Innistrad – where monsters like vampires and werewolves are part of everyday life. She uses more traditional necromancy, while her brother Stitcher Geralf resurrects the undead through scientific means. Their sibling rivalry is always present in the stories where they appear, though Gisa and Geralf will work together when they must.
In this deck, however, Gisa takes center stage. Her ability has you sacrifice a creature, converting its power into even more Zombie tokens. This plays into the two themes of the deck: zombie typal and sacrifice. 

Your typal support rewards you for having a deck loaded with the same types of creatures. You have creatures like Death Baron that strengthen your whole army, Graveborn Muse to draw extra cards, and Diregraf Colossus to make even more zombies. 

Then there's the aristocrats aspect of Wretched Ranks. Aristocrats strategies involve sacrificing your own creatures for valuable effects, such as Gisa's activated ability. You'll want to set up first with effects like Vengeful Dead, and get some expendable creatures like Razorlash Transmogrant or your many zombie tokens. 

There are some excellent reprints in Wretched Ranks, making it a solid place to begin your collection for a reasonable price. Undead Warchief and Graveborn Muse were over $10 each before appearing in this deck, with many other zombie support cards in the $5 range as well. Outside of the zombie-specific cards, Ayara, First of Locthwain and Bontu's Monument are excellent for many black decks, and were overdue for reprints. Carrion Feeder and Ghoulcaller Gisa. are zombies or zombie adjacent, but are also excellent cards outside of that dedicated theme. 

Which Cards To Cut From Wretched Ranks

This deck is perfect out-of-the-box for your first entry into Commander or even to learn Magic as a whole. I highly recommend first playing some games with Wretched Ranks without making changes first, just to get the hang of things. Once you're comfortable, I've got some initial cuts you can make. 

  1. Noxious Ghoul
  2. Syphon Flesh
  3. Josu Vess, Lich Knight 
  4. Liliana's Reaver
  5. Moan of the Unhallowed
  6. Marchesa's Decree 
  7. Commander's Sphere
  8. Castle Locthwain

Noxious Ghoul simply must go. This card's extremely powerful in this deck, but with one hiccup – it kills Gisa! If you ever swap the commander to a zombie, you should absolutely consider Noxious Ghoul. For now, it's gone. Next is Syphon Flesh. It's cool for removing multiple creatures and getting zombie tokens out of the deal, but it's too much mana with little control over what creatures actually die.

We're also dropping Josu Vess, Lich Knight and Liliana's Reaver. These are exciting effects, but cost too much mana to really get going. Moan of the Unhallowed is the same cost upfront, and isn't even as fun as those – it's gone too.

Marchesa's Decree is a minor nuisance, but doesn't stop anyone who really wants to attack you. Commander's Sphere  is a decent way to get mana and cash it in later, but we just added Crowded Crypt for a better effect in that style. 

Finally, I'm trimming one land: Castle Locthwain. Since we dropped some high mana cards and replaced them with lower cost cards, I think we can get away with it in this case. Plus, Castle Locthwain's ability simply costs too much mana and life in most cases.

Adding New Cards To Wretched Ranks

With the cuts identified, here are the replacements to help this deck play out even better. 

The first thing we need is some new kicks for Gisa. Both Swiftfoot Boots and Lightning Greaves will give Gisa haste, allowing you to use her ability the same turn she comes into play. These also each have a way to make it impossible to target Gisa, keeping your commander safe. When Gisa doesn't need them, your other creatures will appreciate the haste as well. 

Next, we've got some juicy fodder for Gisa's ability. Gisa creates a zombie token for every point of power on the creature you sacrifice, so we want high power at a low mana cost. It doesn't matter that Rotting Regisaur has a drawback – it's not sticking around long enough to matter. Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant has no ability at all, but is just as good for fueling Gisa. Ebondeath, Dracolich is a bit lower on power, but is easy to keep playing turn after turn. As a bonus, both Rotting Regisaur and Ebondeath are zombies to work with the rest of your deck's plan. 

Crowded Crypt is an amazing way to get more mana early on, then cash it in for a ton of zombies later. Tragic Slip is a simple but highly effective way to remove a problematic creature. Finally, we're adding Mirkwood Bats to really capitalize on Gisa's ability. You'll trigger the Bats with Gisa and cards like Grave Titan, and you can then sacrifice all your tokens to something like Carrion Feeder for an explosive game-ending move!

Additional Upgrades and Conclusion

There's always room to keep improving your deck. Today's upgrades are kind on your wallet to help ease you into things with your new deck. In the future, you might consider a few premium upgrades like Liliana, Dreadhorde General for card draw, token generation, and removal – she does it all! Jet Medallion is excellent to reduce the cost of your spells, while Eldrazi Monument makes your army nearly unstoppable for a small fee every turn. 

Down the line, you might want to try branching into other colors. You could always try Gisa and Geralf, bringing the pair together for a blue and black zombie duo. Wilhelt, the Rotcleaver is another excellent choice, or you can branch into a third color with Temmet, Naktamun's Will. Zombies are one of Magic's most beloved types, so they have commanders out there in a wide variety of color combinations – you're sure to find one that speaks to you.

Written By

Tyler Berger

A veteran of Konami event coverage and vocal Skull Servant stan, Tyler Berger also claims to have the best hair in Yu-Gi-Oh. Ask him about that one tournament with Zeta Reticulant. View Full Bio

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration
item.description:
Pokémon|collecting

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from 30th Celebration

Pulls worth celebrating.

By Peter Day

|

Published Sep 15, 2026

|

10 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

It doesn't even feel like hyperbole to call 30th Celebration the most-hyped Pokémon TCG set of all time.

Releasing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 all across the world, 30th Celebration represents the culmination of an unprecedented year for Pokémon cards. With the popularity of Pokémon cards reaching never-before-seen heights in 2026, 30th Celebration is channeling all of that excitement and expectation into a single expansion. More people are opening Pokémon cards than ever before, and this is the set they most want to rip.

So, which cards are fans hoping to find in 30th Celebration? The honest answer is simply, "all of them." With its tidy set size, historical significance, and seemingly generous pull rates, 30th Celebration practically demands to be collected into master sets containing one of every card in the expansion. Some pulls will be rarer than others, but each one will be a crucial piece in somebody's collection, and every rarity contains cards with special significance.

For example: did you notice that the Rares in 30th Celebration are the 18 Legendary mascot Pokémon from the nine generations of Pokémon games? (With Mew and Mewtwo subbed in for Gen I.)

But it's tough to hold "everything" in your head while you're ripping packs. So to help you organize your Keep and Trade piles this week, we've put together a list of a few extra-special cards that fans are eager to get their hands on. These are the cards that everybody wants from the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration set.

#10 Unown

The Common-rarity Unown won't be on most collectors' radars. If you're a player though, its Mysterious Signal attack may already be giving you flashbacks to meta-defining cards like Iron Hands ex and Arceus & Dialga & Palkia-GX.

Any Pokémon card that lets you cheat ahead in the Prize trade has a good chance of being busted. Mysterious Signal will have trouble getting there on its own most of the time (though its 40 damage is more than enough to one-shot Budew), but in combination with cards that let you spread damage counters, it can turn around an otherwise unwinnable game.

Keep an eye out for copies of this simple Common as you're ripping packs of 30th Celebration. You may want to keep it for yourself if you like mingo's colorful art, or the way the Unown spell out "anniversary." If not, you can probably find a player at your local game store who'll be happy to trade for it.

#9 The Yuka Morii Item Cards

Since 1998, Morii has set herself apart as a Pokémon card artist by using a unique medium. Instead of illustrating Pokémon, she sculpts them out of clay and photographs them using practical backgrounds, often in nature. 

With over 200 cards to her name, odds are high that you've encountered a Morii card yourself in the wild. But this is her first time lending her beloved style to highly playable Item cards like Poké Pad and Ultra Ball, both of which are basically mandatory to compete in Standard.

Collectors who follow Yuka Morii's work will need all three of these Item cards asap, and more than a few players will want to swap Morii's Item cards into all their decks going forward. Every player who needs a playset creates the same demand as four collectors who want one each, so there's a decent chance that these Item cards will be more valuable than you'd expect. If you're not planning to play with them, it won't be hard to find someone who is.

#8 Every "Pikachu Rare" Pikachu

Every booster pack of 30th Celebration comes with one of 30 unique "Pikachu Rare" cards, each featuring a different artist's take on the world's foremost electric mouse. Because they're numbered out of 30, fans will naturally want to collect 'em all, making them all more valuable by association.

Especially in the early days of 30th Celebration, everyone's first priority will be finding their personal favorite Pikachu Rare. The internet fell in love with OKACHEKE's squishy-cheeked Pikachu early on during the reveals of 30th Celebration, so that one's going to be especially sought-after. But fans may also gravitate toward Pikachu 12/30 by USGMEN, the artist behind Bubble Mew. Or Ken Sugimori's redraw of his iconic Pikachu from Base Set. Or the trippy Pikachu by fan-favorite artist Shinji Kanda.

Whatever Pikachu Rare you pull, it's going to be the exact one someone else is looking for.

#7 The Illustration Rare Legendary Birds

Some of the most desirable Pokémon cards of the 2020s have been connected art cards, where each card forms a piece of a larger illustration. And in 30th Celebration, we're getting a triptych of the most iconic Pokémon trio of all time.

The three Kanto Legendary Birds each have an Illustration Rare in 30th Celebration, which combine to form a colorful cloudscape illustration by mashu, the same artist behind the Bulbasaur connected artwork trio from Mega Evolution. 

Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres have appeared as a connected art trio before, way back in 2009's Supreme Victors. Those are now some of the most valuable cards the legendary birds have ever received, which should give you a good indication of how popular these new connected art cards will be.

#6 Special Illustration Rare Greninja ex

With most modern Pokémon sets, the top of everyone's wishlist is filled with Special Illustration Rares (SIRs), the highest-rarity cards that spotlight each artist's unique style and each Pokémon's unique personality. 30th Celebration includes even more high-rarity prizes to chase than a typical set, but it's still chock-full of gorgeous SIRs that collectors are eager to find.

Other SIRs in 30th Celebration like Sylveon ex might end up carrying a higher price, but the Special Illustration Rare that everybody wants is Greninja ex. Not only has Greninja sneaked its way into the upper echelons of many Pokémon popularity polls, but this card's Stealthy Slash attack can assassinate Benched Pokémon out of nowhere, making this card an exciting find for players and collectors alike.

#5 Classic Collection Gengar (Prime)

Back in 2021, when Pokémon was celebrating its 25th year, the anniversary set Celebrations commemorated that history with a special subset called Classic Collection. This subset consisted of 25 iconic cards from the history of the Pokémon TCG, reprinted in their original style with the 25th anniversary logo.

Five years later, we're getting a new Classic Collection as a 30-card subset in 30th Celebration.

Most of the reprints this time weren't included in the Classic Collection five years ago, so only time will tell which ones end up being the most popular. Will it be the reprint of Shinji Kanda's Magikarp, which outperformed everyone's expectations to become the top chase card in Paldea Evolved? Or the reprint of Shining Celebi, whose original version goes for thousands of dollars?

For my money, we should expect great things from Gengar Prime. Every Gengar card on the market has been on an absolute tear over the past three years, including the original Gengar Prime, which went from $100 at the beginning of 2024 to over $1000 today. Heck, Gengar's so popular that people have tried to sell cards from other games by misidentifying it. No Gengar card can be overlooked in today's market.

#4 Day and Night Special Illustration Rare Pikachu ex

Earlier this year, the internet went a little nuts over Pokémon cards that featured "cameos" by other Pokémon who aren't included in the card's name.

The Pokémon Company sure knows how to please its audience. These two cards represent the entire 30th Celebration set in microcosm, complete with all the big-name Pokémon who're present in the set, and the daytime/nighttime theme that runs through all of 30th Celebration's visuals. With literally dozens of cameos, these SIRs form a natural capstone to 30th Celebration.

But every good concert has an encore, and 30th Celebration has a few chase cards that go beyond the set's "natural" apex.

#3 Classic Collection Charizard

Most of the cards in the 30th Celebration Classic Collection haven't been reprinted since their original set. But one card had to be the exception.

It wouldn't be a Pokémon anniversary set without an homage to Base Set Charizard, possibly the most famous trading card in history. Finding (and likely losing) this card sparked a lifelong obsession with Pokémon cards in an entire generation of fans. Decades later, we're still swimming through the wake this card left behind.

Nobody can return to the past, but we can tear open a fresh card wrapper in 2026 and find Mitsuhiro Arita's iconic illustration roaring back at us. No Pokémon fan will want to leave 30th Celebration behind before they've experienced that. 

#2 Futuristic Rare Mewtwo ex

Anniversaries are a time to look forward as well as back. To celebrate what might come in the next 30+ years of the Pokémon TCG, TPCi commissioned famed Japanese artist YOSHIROTTEN to define the look for a new rarity: Futuristic Rare.

(Personally, these don't look very "futuristic" to me. But I appreciate them more with the context of YOSHIROTTEN's 2018 FUTURE NATURE exhibition, which used the extremes of the visible spectrum to explore the theme of "seeing the invisible.") 

Fans have been waiting for these cards since Pokémon Day 2026 in February, before this anniversary set had a name. We don't yet know how hard they'll be to pull, but if The Pokémon Company follows the precedent set by similar one-off rarities like Black White Rare, Futuristic Rares will be extremely scarce—and therefore, valuable.

#1 Futuristic Rare Mew ex

While either of Futuristic Rares in 30th Celebration will be incredible pulls, Mew ex will likely be the more desirable of the two. Part of that comes down to its brighter color scheme, and to the way Mew has come to symbolize "the unobtainable" for Pokéman fans, as the only Gen I Pokémon that couldn't be captured by playing the original video games normally.

It also helps that Mew ex is the strongest new card in 30th Celebration. With its Memory Helix Ability, Mew ex can copy the attacks of any three-Prize Mega Pokémon ex while only giving up two Prizes itself. That's the same kind of Prize-cheating that makes Unown so dangerous, on a Pokémon that can slot easily into decks of any Energy type.

Editor's Note: This article originally ended here, but The Pokémon Company kept one more group of cards a secret until 30th Celebration released. Now that they've been revealed, the cards that everybody most wants from 30th Celebration are...

#0 The Three RGB Mew Cards

Like Mew itself in the original video games, these cards were originally just sketchy-sounding rumors. As early as July, a streamer opening 30th Celebration packs appeared to find a parallel Mew card with art credited to YOSHIROTTEN and a collector number of B/RGB.

This sparked a small firestorm of controversy over whether the card was actually real. Skeptics noted that the card didn't have the 30th Anniversary stamp common to all the other cards in both 30th Celebration and the 30th Celebration Classic Collection.

Now, the skeptics (myself among them) have to eat their words. The number of copies that have been found around the world are too numerous and similar to one another to be faked. While Mew R/RGB, Mew G/RGB, and Mew B/RGB have yet to be added to Pokémon's official card database or 30th Celebration marketing pages, it appears that The Pokémon Company just wants to keep an air of mystery around these exceptionally rare cards.

As Pokémon's best-kept secret in decades, the RGB Mew cards are the ultimate chase cards of 30th Celebration.
